controls.name: missing_attempts_validation
controls.description: Forgets the 'attempts must be a positive integer' validation entirely. With attempts=0 the loop body never runs, `last_exc` stays None, and `raise last_exc` raises TypeError('exceptions must derive from BaseException') instead of the required ValueError - a realistic case of an agent implementing the happy-path retry logic and skipping the edge-case input validation called out in the docstring.

controls.name: off_by_one_extra_attempt
controls.description: Off-by-one: loops range(attempts + 1), i.e. makes ONE MORE attempt than requested. Invisible when the first success happens before the last allowed attempt, but when every call fails it re-raises the exception from attempt (attempts + 1) instead of the last exception from attempt `attempts`, and calls make_coro() one extra time.

controls.name: reused_coroutine_object
controls.description: Calls make_coro() exactly once, before the loop, and re-awaits the SAME coroutine object on every retry instead of calling make_coro() fresh each attempt. A plausible misreading of the 'zero-argument callable' contract by an agent that only skims the docstring. Once a coroutine has been awaited to completion (return or raise), awaiting it again raises RuntimeError('cannot reuse already awaited coroutine') instead of actually retrying, so any test requiring more than one attempt fails or raises the wrong exception.

controls.name: swallows_base_exceptions
controls.description: Security/robustness-relevant near-miss: broadens `except Exception` to `except BaseException`, so asyncio.CancelledError (a BaseException subclass, not an Exception subclass, since Python 3.8) is caught, swallowed, and retried instead of propagating immediately. This is a realistic 'be extra safe' widening a partial fix might introduce, but it breaks cooperative task cancellation/timeouts: a caller that cancels a task stuck inside retry_call would have the cancellation silently absorbed and the retry loop kept running, which can hang shutdown or hold resources instead of stopping - an availability/DoS-adjacent bug. Every existing hidden test only raises Exception subclasses (ValueError/RuntimeError), so this mutant is expected to slip past the current hidden suite undetected, which is itself the finding this control is meant to surface.

controls.name: recursive_retry
controls.description: Structurally different but behaviorally equivalent to the reference: recursion with an explicit remaining-attempts counter and a bare `raise` on the last frame, instead of the reference's for-loop with a last_exc accumulator variable. Same observable behavior (result on first success, last exception re-raised on exhaustion, no extra calls after success, ValueError on attempts<=0). Should be ACCEPTED.

controls.description: Division uses Python's floor-division operator (//) instead of true division (/), a plausible slip when porting arithmetic logic from a language where '/' truncates. '7/2' returns 3.0 instead of 3.5. Everything else (precedence, associativity, unary minus, parentheses) is copied verbatim from the reference, isolating this single defect.

controls.name: right_associative_subtraction
controls.description: Re-introduces the real pre-Phase-35 defect this task was patched for: parse_expression/parse_term fold from the right instead of the left, so '10-2-3' evaluates as 10-(2-3)=11 instead of (10-2)-3=5, and '8/2/2' as 8/(2/2)=8 instead of 2. Unary minus handling is left correct (copied verbatim from the reference) so this control isolates only the associativity regression. The hidden suite's dedicated left-associativity tests must reject this.

controls.name: unary_minus_non_leading_crash
controls.description: Realistic partial fix for unary minus: parse_factor only special-cases a leading '+'/'-' when it is the very first token of the whole expression (self.pos == 0), instead of recognizing unary sign at every factor position. '-3+2' still works, but '1+-2', '6/-2', '2--3', and '3*(-2)' all raise ValueError because the parser reaches a bare '-' where it expects a number. Matches the prior real defect's 'unary-minus crashing' symptom.

controls.name: eval_based_implementation
controls.description: Task-specific, security-relevant near-miss: computes the answer with Python's eval() instead of a real parser, which the task prose explicitly forbids ('Do NOT use eval()') because handing attacker-influenced text to eval() is an arbitrary-code-execution risk, not a style nit. Python's own +,-,*,/ operators happen to share the same precedence, left-associativity, and unary-minus semantics the task specifies, so on every benign input the hidden suite exercises this produces byte-identical results to a correct parser. Expected reject: this is exactly the kind of spec-violating shortcut a naive or corner-cutting agent might submit. If the purely behavioral hidden suite accepts it, that is a genuine benchmark-integrity gap (nothing in the grading verifies the 'no eval()' constraint), not an authoring mistake.

controls.name: shunting_yard_rpn
controls.description: Structurally different but behaviorally equivalent correct implementation: a shunting-yard algorithm that converts tokens to RPN (with unary +/- represented as distinct, higher-precedence, right-associative pseudo-operators 'u+'/'u-' resolved via a two-stack shunting yard) and then evaluates the RPN with a single value stack. No recursive-descent grammar, no _Parser class, no eval(). Correctly preserves left-associativity for +-*/ and correct unary-minus semantics at every position (leading, after another operator, and inside parentheses).

controls.name: dotdot_literal_check
controls.description: Rejects any individual part containing a literal '..' segment (plus any absolute component), but never normalizes-and-compares against base at all. This over-rejects a legitimate '..' that still resolves within base (e.g. "reports/../public"), because it looks only at the raw, pre-join part text rather than the resolved path. A plausible 'forgot the allowed edge case' fix: the author reasoned '..' is always dangerous and blocked it outright instead of checking containment.

controls.name: normalized_dotdot_token_check
controls.description: Checks for absolute components, then normalizes the joined path and rejects it only if a literal '..' token survives normalization. Since posixpath.normpath collapses every resolvable '..' for an absolute base, this check almost never fires: e.g. base "/srv/data", part "../etc/passwd" normalizes straight to "/srv/etc/passwd" with no '..' left, so the escape sails through silently. A realistic 'missing validation' bug: the author normalizes but never actually compares the result against base.

controls.name: wrong_exception_type
controls.description: Containment logic is otherwise correct (mirrors the reference's normalize-then-prefix-check), but raises PermissionError instead of the required ValueError on an escape. A plausible slip: the author copied an access-control pattern from elsewhere in the codebase and kept its exception type instead of switching to ValueError as the task spec requires. Every hidden test that does pytest.raises(ValueError) on an escaping input fails because PermissionError propagates uncaught.

controls.name: prefix_startswith_no_separator
controls.description: Reintroduces the historical prefix-collision bug this task's reference used to have: containment is enforced via a naive norm_joined.startswith(norm_base) with NO trailing-separator check. A sibling directory that merely shares a name prefix (e.g. "/srv/data-other") is wrongly treated as being under base "/srv/data", because the string "/srv/data-other/file.txt" literally starts with the string "/srv/data". This is exactly the task-specific security near-miss a partial or naive fix of safe_join is likely to reproduce.

controls.name: segment_stack_resolution
controls.description: Structurally different but behaviorally equivalent correct solution: instead of normalizing the whole joined string with posixpath.normpath and then doing a str.startswith prefix compare, this walks base's segments plus every part's segments onto one explicit list-stack (the same left-to-right resolution normpath performs internally), allowing a transient climb above base that comes back down before the walk ends, and only checks the FINAL resolved position against base -- via list-prefix comparison, not string prefix -- so it also can never be fooled by a same-prefix sibling like '/srv/data-other'.

controls.description: A string-expansion implementation (expand each subtractive pair to its additive equivalent, then sum digit-by-digit) that omits the XC -> LXXXX expansion rule -- a realistic oversight since 90 is the least memorable of the six subtractive pairs. XC (90) is summed as X+C=110 instead, and MCMXCIV -- which contains an embedded XC -- comes out 20 too high (2014 instead of 1994). controls.name: off_by_one_comparison
controls.description: Forward-scanning implementation that uses <= instead of < when deciding whether the current numeral is smaller than its neighbor, so two adjacent numerals of EQUAL value are wrongly treated as a subtractive pair and cancel out instead of adding (III -> -1, LVIII -> 54). A very plausible off-by-one when writing the lookahead comparison. Standard non-repeating subtractive forms like IV/IX still come out correct, so this control is only caught by the repeated-numeral hidden tests.

controls.description: A pair-lookup implementation with a realistic copy/paste typo: the two-letter keys for 9 and 900 are transposed ("XI" instead of "IX", "MC" instead of "CM"), so the actual subtractive forms IX and CM never match the table and fall through to plain digit summation (IX -> 11, CM -> 1100). controls.name: forward_lookahead

Different iteration direction, different loop state; produces identical results for every well-formed Roman numeral (the two approaches only diverge on malformed/ambiguous strings outside the task's spec, e.g. "IIX").
